## Mexico City's National Palace: visits subject to availability

The [National Palace in Mexico City](/mexico/place/national-palace-mexico-city/) occupies the eastern side of Zócalo Square. Its long façade forms part of the historic city centre. Inside, the building is known for its courtyards and Diego Rivera murals, but it remains an active government site. Entry depends on official events and access arrangements.

For this reason, tours must distinguish **walking around the square and viewing the building from outside**, which can be planned as part of a city tour, from **entering the palace**, which requires separate confirmation. Here you will find {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} in which the National Palace is a possible stop rather than a guaranteed interior visit.

## Which trips offer an opportunity to see the palace?

### Religious journey through Mexico: the historic centre and churches

The [seven-day religious journey through Mexico](/mexico/tour/mexico-religious-journey/) devotes one day to the capital's historic centre. The itinerary includes [Zócalo](/mexico/place/mexico-city-zocalo/), Santo Domingo Church, the Metropolitan Cathedral and the National Palace, followed by Garibaldi Square.

The main purpose of this day is to discover Mexico City's religious and cultural heritage. Entry to the National Palace is explicitly conditional on access being permitted. Even if the group cannot go inside, the programme still includes churches and walks through historic streets. Exact dates and the order of visits are available on the tour page.

### "Central America: Eight Countries in 26 Days"

The [26-day Central America itinerary](/multi-country/tour/central-america-8-countries-26-days/) begins in Mexico City, then continues through Central American countries to Panama. Its sightseeing day in the capital includes Zócalo, the cathedral, Templo Mayor, Chapultepec and the National Museum of Anthropology.

The National Palace is mentioned as **an opportunity to view its interiors and murals if entry is permitted**. There is no reason to rearrange the geography of a 26-day expedition for this single stop. The decision is made within the city sightseeing day and depends on actual access. The main value of this itinerary is discovering several countries in sequence, not a guaranteed visit to a government building.

| Itinerary | Context of the palace visit |
| --- | --- |
| [Religious journey](/mexico/tour/mexico-religious-journey/) | Historic centre, churches and Garibaldi Square |
| [Eight countries in 26 days](/multi-country/tour/central-america-8-countries-26-days/) | A cultural day in Mexico City before travelling onwards |

## What if visitors cannot enter the palace?

The sightseeing day still has plenty to offer without access to the interiors. From the square, visitors can view the palace and its place within the Zócalo complex. Nearby are the Metropolitan Cathedral and the Templo Mayor archaeological site. Together, they illuminate different aspects of the city's history: government, religion and the pre-colonial past.

Before your visit, confirm whether entry is possible on the actual excursion date. Standard museum opening hours do not determine access to an active government building. If entry is restricted, it would be misleading to replace a promise to see the murals with a vague claim that "we will visit the palace anyway". Instead, distinguish the exterior view from the conditional interior programme.

If your main interest is Mexican history more broadly, also compare [cultural and historical tours in Mexico](/interests/culture-and-history/tours/mexico/) and [general tours of the country](/mexico/tour/). They let you choose by the time spent in the capital and at other attractions, rather than focusing on a single site whose entry may be restricted.

## Choosing between the two itineraries

The seven-day tour makes sense for someone primarily interested in pilgrimage, Masses, churches and the history of Mexican religious culture. The National Palace may complement the day without defining its purpose.

The 26-day itinerary suits travellers who want to cross several countries and spend some time in Mexico City as part of a longer journey. Maintaining the pace is particularly important: extra visits must fit around the onward travel schedule. Check the detailed inclusions and guiding languages in the [eight-country itinerary](/multi-country/tour/central-america-8-countries-26-days/).

## Frequently asked questions about the National Palace

### Does a tour guarantee entry to the National Palace?

No. Both itineraries make access to the interior conditional on current rules. Listing the palace among potential stops is not the same as providing a confirmed admission ticket.

### Can I see the palace when its interior is closed?

Its façade is visible from Zócalo Square. Viewing the building from outside is different from entering the courtyards and seeing the murals, so confirm exactly what the excursion includes.

### Should I plan an entire sightseeing day around the palace?

For a general introduction to Mexico City, it is better to combine the palace with Zócalo and other landmarks in the historic centre. That way, the day remains worthwhile even if access is restricted.

### Which itinerary spends more time at religious sites?

The specialised [seven-day pilgrimage itinerary](/mexico/tour/mexico-religious-journey/) focuses on churches and religious culture. The 26-day tour treats Mexico City as the starting point of a much larger journey through Central America.

## Oaxaca: Zapotec history, city markets and traditional crafts

Oaxaca lies in a mountain valley in southern [Mexico](/mexico/). Its appeal to travellers comes from several intertwined stories: a colonial city, pre-Columbian monuments, living craft traditions and a remarkably varied regional cuisine. It is well suited to a trip with several days devoted to culture, archaeology and workshops.

In 1987, UNESCO inscribed Oaxaca's historic centre and the archaeological site of Monte Albán together as a World Heritage property. They are two separate locations: the city streets can be explored on foot, while the archaeological complex requires its own excursion.

## The historic centre: Zócalo and Santo Domingo

The city centre retains squares, arcades, monastic complexes and low stone buildings. Zócalo, the main square, remains a focus of everyday life, while the Santo Domingo complex is an important architectural landmark and museum site.

Oaxaca's buildings reflect the region's seismic activity: thick walls and relatively low construction are characteristic features of its historic centre. On a walking tour, allow time for the neighbouring streets, workshops and markets rather than visiting only the two best-known squares.

The markets offer a chance to discover local spices, chocolate, handicrafts and prepared foods. Opening hours, selections and the degree to which each market caters to tourists differ, so it helps to choose a few specific places before setting out.

## Monte Albán: an ancient city above the valley

Monte Albán occupies a hilltop site outside the modern city centre. The archaeological complex is associated with Zapotec civilisation and later cultural periods. Surviving features include platforms, stairways, plazas, burials and a ball court.

UNESCO regards Monte Albán as one of the Oaxaca Valley's most important archaeological sites. A guide is particularly helpful in explaining the purposes of the structures and the settlement's development. Slopes, exposed spaces and strong sunshine call for comfortable footwear and sun protection.

Set aside a separate part of the day for this excursion. Combining a comprehensive archaeological visit with numerous city museums would be rushed.

## Craft villages and regional cuisine

The area around Oaxaca is known for carved and painted wooden *alebrijes*, black pottery and textiles. Workshops offer opportunities to observe how objects are made and to meet local artisan families. Visits to San Antonio Arrazola, San Bartolo Coyotepec or Teotitlán del Valle require advance transport planning.

Food experiences include varieties of mole, maize-based dishes, chocolate and local markets. Mezcal production is also connected with agave and the state's traditions; tastings for adults should be arranged separately, with transport in mind. Oaxaca is worth visiting even without that activity.

Our [food and wine travel section](/interests/food-and-wine/) lets you compare other destinations where local cooking and production genuinely form part of the itinerary.

## Which Ada Tours itineraries include Oaxaca?

For an introduction to the region, consider ["Oaxaca: A Five-Day City Break"](/mexico/tour/oaxaca-city-break-5-days/). It includes four nights in Oaxaca and visits to Monte Albán, craft workshops, Mitla and Hierve el Agua. This is a focused itinerary that spends most of its time within one region.

["Viva Mexico: Mexico City, Oaxaca and Yucatán in 12 Days"](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/) links Oaxaca with several other areas of the country. It suits those wanting a wider cultural journey who are prepared to spend more time travelling. Do not assume that the excursions on both tours are identical: compare the exact daily programme, included services and transport.

If you want to extend your route independently through central Mexico, explore [Puebla](/mexico/place/puebla/) and [Mexico City with Teotihuacán](/mexico/place/mexico-city-and-teotihuacan/).

## Frequently asked questions about Oaxaca

### Which should I see first: Oaxaca or Monte Albán?

Begin with the historic centre to discover the city, then make a separate excursion to Monte Albán. This allows you to appreciate the contrast between colonial and pre-Columbian history.

### How many days do I need in Oaxaca?

Allow at least two full, meaningful days for the city centre and an archaeological excursion. If you want to visit craft workshops and the surrounding region, a four- or five-day programme is more convenient.

### Is Oaxaca suitable for a food-focused trip?

Yes. The city and state are known for their regional cuisine, markets and artisan production. Choose specific visits and workshops rather than relying on a generic "food tour" label.

## Which tours visit Oaxaca?

[Oaxaca](/mexico/place/oaxaca/) is an excellent destination for a journey focused on Zapotec history, handicrafts and local cuisine. It is important, however, to distinguish a visit to Oaxaca city from a brief stop somewhere else in the state of the same name. The itineraries in this collection include **Oaxaca as part of their main route**, rather than offering it only as an optional excursion.

You can choose from {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}}. On the ["Oaxaca: Five-Day City Break"](/mexico/tour/oaxaca-city-break-5-days/), all overnight stays are in one city. ["Viva Mexico"](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/) combines Oaxaca with Mexico City and Yucatán. Both tours allow time for the city itself, ancient monuments and traditional workshops.

| Itinerary | Main difference |
|---|---|
| Oaxaca, 5 days | One hotel base, excursions from the city |
| Viva Mexico, 12 days | Mexico City, Oaxaca and Yucatán |

{{catalog.tourTable:tour_mexico_oaxaca_city_break_five_days,tour_source_viva_meksika}}

Time spent in the city is a separate consideration from the overall duration. The five-day itinerary includes **four nights in Oaxaca**. The 12-day itinerary also allocates four nights to Oaxaca, while its other stages take place in Mexico City and Mérida. The longer tour therefore covers more places but does not provide more days in Oaxaca itself.

## Five days based in Oaxaca

The short itinerary begins with a welcome at Oaxaca Airport and a private transfer to the hotel. There is free time after check-in. The next day includes a guided walk through the historic centre, with Zócalo Square, the Santo Domingo area, pedestrian streets and markets. A separate description of the [Oaxaca walking tour](/mexico/oaxaca/oaxaca-walking-tour/) gives you a clearer idea of this day before booking. The walk lasts four hours.

Day three is devoted to [Monte Albán](/mexico/place/monte-alban/) and nearby craft villages. Monte Albán, once a centre of Zapotec civilisation, stands above the valley. Oaxaca's historic centre and this archaeological site were jointly inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. After visiting the monuments, travellers see the production of painted wooden figures in [San Antonio Arrazola](/mexico/place/san-antonio-arrazola/) and black pottery in [San Bartolo Coyotepec](/mexico/place/san-bartolo-coyotepec/). The [Monte Albán and craft villages excursion](/mexico/monte-alban/monte-alban-craft-villages-tour/) describes this day's experiences in detail.

Day four explores another part of the valley. It starts with [Mitla](/mexico/place/mitla/) and its characteristic geometric stone mosaics, followed by weaving workshops in [Teotitlán del Valle](/mexico/place/teotitlan-del-valle/), the natural mineral formations of [Hierve el Agua](/mexico/place/hierve-el-agua/) and an introduction to mezcal production. This is a substantial excursion lasting nine to ten hours, not a short walk near the hotel. See the separate [Mitla, Hierve el Agua and mezcal itinerary](/mexico/mitla/mitla-hierve-el-agua-mescal-tour/) for more details.

On day five, the trip ends with a private airport transfer. This arrangement suits travellers keen to discover several sides of the region while keeping the same hotel for all four nights.

### What is included in the five-day itinerary?

According to the [specific tour conditions](/mexico/tour/oaxaca-city-break-5-days/), the package includes four nights' accommodation with breakfast, airport–hotel transfers, scheduled group excursions and a bilingual English- and Spanish-speaking guide. One lunch is also listed, although the day on which it is provided needs to be confirmed alongside the excursion arrangements. Other meals, personal expenses and additional entertainment are excluded.

When comparing prices, read the tour's SGL, DBL and TPL accommodation conditions carefully. Its pricing table lists different rates for these options, so the lowest figure cannot be assumed to apply to every room arrangement. Check the hotel name and exact dates against the product terms.

## Twelve days: Oaxaca within a journey across Mexico

["Viva Mexico"](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/) is designed for travellers who want to add the capital and Yucatán's archaeological sites to Oaxaca. The opening days take place in Mexico City, with its historic centre, Teotihuacán, the Xochimilco canals and the southern districts. The itinerary then heads to Oaxaca. A flight or an overland journey, potentially stopping in Puebla, is described; the precise transport and associated costs must be matched to the chosen tour option.

The main Oaxaca experiences on the longer itinerary partly overlap with the five-day break: a city walk, Monte Albán and craft villages, Mitla, weaving workshops, Hierve el Agua and mezcal. The journey then continues to [Mérida](/mexico/place/merida/) and Yucatán's attractions. Its route includes Uxmal, cenotes and Chichén Itzá, ending in the direction of the Riviera Maya.

Travel between regions is what distinguishes this longer tour. It involves domestic transfers and several hotel bases. Before choosing, check which air tickets are included, which flights cost extra, how transfers are organised and what happens on the final day. The 12-day trip suits a first introduction to several of Mexico's cultural regions, while the five-day itinerary offers a self-contained stay dedicated to Oaxaca.

## Experiences that deserve enough time

To choose between tours, assess what happens each day rather than counting place names.

**History.** [Monte Albán](/mexico/place/monte-alban/) and [Mitla](/mexico/place/mitla/) reveal different approaches to Zapotec architecture. At Monte Albán, the scale of the open spaces and the ancient city's location above the valley are particularly striking. At Mitla, the focus is on geometric ornament made from precisely fitted stones covering the buildings. A guide helps explain the differences between these sites.

**Crafts.** [Alebrijes in Arrazola](/mexico/place/san-antonio-arrazola/), [Coyotepec black pottery](/mexico/place/san-bartolo-coyotepec/) and [Teotitlán woollen textiles](/mexico/place/teotitlan-del-valle/) come from distinct craft traditions. Visiting all three allows you to compare materials and watch artisans at work. It is another reason to leave enough time for excursions instead of planning an endless series of stops.

**Nature and food.** [Hierve el Agua](/mexico/place/hierve-el-agua/) features mineral formations and pools amid the mountains; a mezcal stop introduces travellers to agave and how the spirit is produced. These places call for different preparations: walking shoes, sun protection and moderation with tastings before further travel. Itineraries that include workshops and mezcal may also appeal to people interested in [Mexico's food and wine tours](/interests/food-and-wine/tours/mexico/).

## Choosing between the two itineraries

If you have already visited Mexico City and Yucatán, or have around five days for the entire trip, choose the itinerary based in Oaxaca. Its main excursions are organised around one city. If this is your first visit to Mexico and you want to explore several distant regions in one journey, compare the complete [12-day itinerary](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/).

There are practical differences, too. On the five-day trip, airport transfers are private, while excursions on days two through four are group activities. "Viva Mexico" has more complicated transport arrangements because it involves travel within the country, with flights and overland alternatives specified in its own programme. The labels "private" and "group" cannot be applied to one entire product merely because they describe a service on the other.

Before booking, check the dates, pricing basis, hotels, guide languages and actual excursion inclusions. Clothing suitable for different conditions is useful when moving between Mexican regions. In Oaxaca, prepare for sun exposure at open archaeological sites, light rain during the wet season and uneven stone surfaces. Confirm monument opening hours and access to natural areas closer to your travel dates.

For further choices, browse the [general Mexico tour catalogue](/mexico/tour/) and the [cultural and historical tours collection](/interests/culture-and-history/tours/mexico/). These cover more itineraries and do not automatically imply a visit to Oaxaca.

## Frequently asked questions

### How many nights are spent in Oaxaca on each tour?

The short trip includes four nights in Oaxaca. "Viva Mexico" also allocates four nights to Oaxaca, but lasts 12 days overall because it includes Mexico City and Yucatán.

### Can I visit Monte Albán and Mitla in one day?

On both itineraries, they are scheduled for different excursion days. Monte Albán is combined with craft villages, while Mitla is visited with weaving workshops, Hierve el Agua and mezcal. Combining everything into one day is not an included service.

### Are all excursions on the five-day tour private?

No. The airport transfers are specified as private. Excursion transport and walks on days two to four are described as group services, with guiding in English and Spanish.

### Is there time to explore Oaxaca independently?

There is free time after arrival on the first day. After the sightseeing walk on day two, guests can also visit markets, art galleries or cafés on their own. Additional workshops and special activities are not automatically included in the base package.

### How can I combine Oaxaca with Mexico City and Yucatán?

That combination is already available in ["Viva Mexico"](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/): the capital comes first, followed by Oaxaca, then Mérida, archaeological sites and cenotes in Yucatán. Flights, alternative ground transfers and the exact final transfer must be chosen according to that tour's conditions.

## Basilica of Our Lady of Ocotlán: a shrine near Tlaxcala

The Basilica of Our Lady of Ocotlán (Basílica de Nuestra Señora de Ocotlán) stands near [Tlaxcala](/mexico/place/tlaxcala/) in central Mexico. Its two bell towers, red-brick surfaces and intricately carved white façade make it instantly recognisable. An active Catholic shrine and a striking example of Mexican Baroque architecture, it draws visitors interested in the venerated image of the Virgin Mary, sacred art and the history of local pilgrimage.

Ocotlán is easy to combine with other shrines in the region. Yet it has its own story, and appreciating it deserves time not only to photograph the façade but also to explore the interior thoughtfully.

## The tradition of Our Lady of Ocotlán

According to Church tradition, in 1541 a local young man named Juan Diego encountered the Virgin Mary near San Lorenzo hill. The story describes a spring whose water was taken to sick people and directions to a tree where a wooden image of the Virgin Mary was later found. This is **a religious tradition**, not a documented sequence of historical events.

The name Juan Diego also appears in accounts of Our Lady of Guadalupe, but Ocotlán has a distinct local devotion, its own sacred image and a shrine in Tlaxcala. For pilgrims, the difference matters: the [Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe](/mexico/place/basilica-of-guadalupe/) and Ocotlán are separate stops on a religious tour of Mexico.

Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) dates the beginning of construction of the present church to 1670. The traditional date of the apparition and the construction date of the surviving building thus belong to different periods.

## What to notice in the architecture and interior

Outside, the contrast of materials makes the greatest impression. Two towers with red-brick surfaces flank the tall white entrance portal, whose carved decoration surrounds the doorway and upper levels. The façade rewards viewing from several points in front of the church, from its overall silhouette to the figures, columns and individual ornaments.

Inside, attention turns to the altar area and the wooden image of Our Lady. A distinctive part of the interior is the **camarín**, a chamber associated with dressing the venerated image before religious ceremonies. This feature helps explain why Ocotlán remains a functioning shrine: its works of art are connected to living liturgical practice.

During a visit, consider three aspects separately: the Baroque treatment of the façade, the decoration of the altars and the continuing tradition of veneration. If Mass or another ceremony is under way, worshippers take priority; ask locally about photography and movement inside the church.

## Including Ocotlán on a Mexico itinerary

On the [7-day religious journey through Mexico](/mexico/tour/mexico-religious-journey/), the stop at the basilica falls on the day travelling through Tlaxcala and Puebla. Travellers also visit the [Shrine of San Miguel del Milagro](/mexico/place/san-miguel-del-milagro/) and the [Monastery of San Francisco in Tlaxcala](/mexico/place/san-francisco-tlaxcala/) before continuing to churches in [Puebla](/mexico/place/puebla/). Mass on this itinerary is scheduled at San Miguel del Milagro; a visit to Ocotlán must not be confused with a promise of a separate Mass inside the basilica.

The same shrines can also be visited on the independent [“Shrines of Tlaxcala, Ocotlán and Puebla” excursion](/mexico/tlaxcala/tlaxcala-ocotlan-puebla-pilgrimage/). It includes the monastery, the Ocotlán shrine, [Puebla Cathedral](/mexico/place/puebla-cathedral/) and the [Chapel of the Rosary](/mexico/place/puebla-santo-domingo-rosary-chapel/). Visiting all these sites on one excursion day makes for a full programme with travel between stops. For an unhurried pilgrimage and private prayer, discuss the length of each visit separately.

More routes featuring religious and architectural landmarks are available among [Mexico's cultural and historical tours](/interests/culture-and-history/tours/mexico/). The themed catalogue presents different itineraries, but the included Masses, visits and services depend on the one you select.

## Visiting an active shrine

It is best to approach the basilica as a living place of worship. Wear clothing appropriate for a religious site, remain quiet near the altar and ask in advance whether the camarín can be visited. Service times, interior access and photography permissions may change; a universal schedule for an independent visit cannot be guaranteed.

If your interest is architectural, a considered look at the façade and principal interior spaces may be enough. If you are making a pilgrimage, specify how you wish to participate in Church life when arranging the itinerary: private prayer, attending an existing Mass or a specially organised programme for your group. These options involve different time requirements and arrangements.

## Frequently asked questions about the Basilica of Ocotlán

### Where is the Basilica of Our Lady of Ocotlán?

It is in the Tlaxcala area of central Mexico. Use [Tlaxcala](/mexico/place/tlaxcala/) and the regional shrine itinerary as reference points when planning your visit.

### Are Ocotlán and Guadalupe the same shrine?

No. They are different Catholic shrines associated with separate traditions, images of Our Lady and places of devotion. On the Ada Tours itinerary, they are distinct stops.

### Can I visit Ocotlán and Puebla on the same day?

Yes. That combination is included in the [Tlaxcala and Puebla excursion](/mexico/tlaxcala/tlaxcala-ocotlan-puebla-pilgrimage/). Independent travellers need to account for road travel, church services and time at each site.

### Is Mass celebrated at Ocotlán on the Ada Tours tour?

On the described [7-day pilgrimage tour](/mexico/tour/mexico-religious-journey/), Mass on the day of the Ocotlán visit is scheduled at San Miguel del Milagro. Attendance at a service in the basilica itself must be arranged separately.

## Which tours include the Basilica of Our Lady of Ocotlán?

The [Basilica of Our Lady of Ocotlán](/mexico/place/ocotlan-basilica/) stands near [Tlaxcala](/mexico/place/tlaxcala/) and is known for its carved white façade, red brickwork and richly decorated Baroque interior. It is both an active shrine and an architectural monument, so a visit needs to take account of religious services and restrictions on access to individual rooms.

Our collection features {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} whose main route includes Ocotlán. The confirmed option is the ["Religious Journey through Mexico: Seven Days"](/mexico/tour/mexico-religious-journey/), scheduled for **1–7 April 2027**. Ocotlán is visited on **day four, 4 April**, alongside other shrines in Tlaxcala and Puebla states.

This itinerary is designed for travellers wishing to combine Catholic pilgrimage with Mexico's colonial churches and history. It is not a substitute for a leisurely independent visit to Ocotlán alone: the same day has several stops, and the group returns to Mexico City in the evening.

## What happens on 4 April?

In the morning, the group departs Mexico City and travels through mountainous country to the [Shrine of San Miguel del Milagro](/mexico/place/san-miguel-del-milagro/), where **Holy Mass** is scheduled. Next come [Tlaxcala](/mexico/place/tlaxcala/), the [Monastery of San Francisco](/mexico/place/san-francisco-tlaxcala/) and the Basilica of Ocotlán. The day continues in [Puebla](/mexico/place/puebla/) with visits to its [cathedral](/mexico/place/puebla-cathedral/) and [Santo Domingo Church with the Chapel of the Rosary](/mexico/place/puebla-santo-domingo-rosary-chapel/).

| Stop | Main purpose |
|---|---|
| San Miguel del Milagro | Holy Mass |
| Tlaxcala | Historic monastery |
| Ocotlán | Basilica and venerated image |
| Puebla | Cathedral and Baroque chapel |

The full sequence is also set out in the separate ["Shrines of Tlaxcala, Ocotlán and Puebla" excursion](/mexico/tlaxcala/tlaxcala-ocotlan-puebla-pilgrimage/). Travel is by private vehicle with an English-speaking guide. Admission to the listed sights is included; access to restricted church areas and service times depend on the shrine's rules.

The group returns to Mexico City that evening. If you choose this itinerary, expect **a substantial sightseeing day with several road journeys**, not an entire day spent inside the basilica.

## Why pilgrims visit the Shrine of Ocotlán

According to Church tradition, devotion to Our Lady of Ocotlán is linked to an apparition of the Virgin Mary to a local resident, Juan Diego Bernardino, in **1541**. The account mentions a spring and an image discovered in a tree. This belongs to religious tradition and should be distinguished from the documented dates of the building's construction.

According to historical materials published by Mexican cultural institutions, construction of the larger shrine began in the late seventeenth century, while later works shaped its Baroque decoration. Outside, the two towers with white stucco details catch the eye. Inside, notable features include the altars, decorative carvings and the **camarín**, a chamber behind the main altar associated with dressing the revered image of Our Lady.

Two details are worth noticing on the tour. First is the contrast between the red-brick surfaces and the light-coloured relief ornament on the façade. Second is the difference between the relatively restrained outer silhouette and the richly decorated interior. For believers, the greatest significance lies in the image of Our Lady and the opportunity to spend quiet time at the shrine.

### Can visitors enter the camarín?

The camarín is one of the complex's best-known artistic spaces, but **unrestricted admission cannot be guaranteed**. Tlaxcala tourism materials recommend visiting with a guide and address access separately. Even when the basilica is open, some rooms may be closed for church events. The Ada Tours itinerary confirms a visit to the shrine, not unrestricted entry to every interior room.

## How the full seven-day pilgrimage is organised

Ocotlán is one stop on a continuous itinerary with **all six nights spent in Mexico City**. This is convenient for the group: luggage stays at the same hotel while excursions to neighbouring towns are made without suitcases.

The [Mexico journey](/mexico/tour/mexico-religious-journey/) includes five Holy Masses. They take place at the Shrine of Our Lady of Guadalupe, Santo Domingo Church in Mexico City, San Miguel del Milagro, Santa Prisca in Taxco and the Church of St James in Tlatelolco. **The visit to Ocotlán is not listed as a separate Mass.**

Before travelling to Tlaxcala, guests explore Mexico City and the [Shrine of Our Lady of Guadalupe](/mexico/place/basilica-of-guadalupe/). The day after Ocotlán, the itinerary takes them to [Cuernavaca](/mexico/place/cuernavaca/) and [Taxco](/mexico/place/taxco/). The final section includes [Teotihuacán](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/) and Tlatelolco. This sequence introduces the religious history of different periods, from early colonial monasteries to major modern pilgrimage centres.

## Accommodation, guiding and conditions

The package includes six nights in a standard room at **Casa Blanca 4\*** or a hotel of a comparable standard, private transfers, an English-speaking guide, scheduled breakfasts and dinners, admission tickets to the listed sights and the celebration of five Masses. Groups of up to 24 travel by minibus; groups of 25 or more travel by tourist coach.

International flights, drinks, personal expenses and tips are excluded. **There is no fixed price on the tour page**, so the cost of a one-day excursion should not be substituted for the price of the entire journey when comparing offers.

Choose clothing appropriate for church services and comfortable shoes, as several historic complexes are visited in one day. At the shrine, take photographs only where permitted. If a service is taking place, worship takes priority over tourist photography.

## Frequently asked questions

### On which day does the tour visit Ocotlán?

On **4 April 2027**, day four of the seven-day itinerary. The excursion starts in Mexico City and includes Tlaxcala, the Basilica of Ocotlán and Puebla.

### Will Holy Mass be celebrated inside the Basilica of Ocotlán?

On the current itinerary, Mass on 4 April is scheduled **at San Miguel del Milagro**. At Ocotlán, the group visits the shrine to learn about its history and decoration.

### Do we need to change hotels to visit Ocotlán?

No. All six nights are spent in Mexico City. The excursion to Tlaxcala, Ocotlán and Puebla returns to the capital the same day.

### Can we spend more time at Ocotlán?

It is possible to discuss the allocation of time when arranging an individual itinerary, but extending the stop would require changes to the other visits on the busy fourth day. The published programme does not include a separate free day in Ocotlán.

### Is this itinerary suitable for someone interested only in Baroque architecture?

Yes, if you are also interested in other historic churches in central Mexico. In addition to Ocotlán, the itinerary visits the [Monastery of San Francisco in Tlaxcala](/mexico/place/san-francisco-tlaxcala/), [Puebla Cathedral](/mexico/place/puebla-cathedral/) and the [Chapel of the Rosary](/mexico/place/puebla-santo-domingo-rosary-chapel/). The complete route and conditions are available on the [tour page](/mexico/tour/mexico-religious-journey/).
